## The "Reproducibility Crisis"

- Reproducibility of [results]{style="color:red"}, not methods
- Clear problems in psychology, social science & biomedicine.
- Do these problems affect ecology?

# Causes

## Reproducibility Crisis: Causes

1. Publication bias against
    - negative results
    - confirmation / "me too" results
2. Misinterpretation of statistics
    - -> high "false discovery rates"

## Publication bias
::: columns
::: {.column width="80%"}
![](images/bem_paper.png)

- Results failed to reproduce in other studies
- Journals [would not publish]{style="color:red"} these "negative" studies
:::
::: {.column width="20%"}
![Bem 2011 "proves pre-cognition".](images/psychic.jpg)
:::
:::

## Publication bias & Dark Matter {background="#43464B" background-image="images/milky-way.jpeg"}
```{r darkmatter}
library(magrittr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
set.seed(456)
y <- rnorm(10000, 0, 33)
# hist(y)
cutoff <- quantile(y, probs = 0.95)

df_dens <- density(y, from = -100, to = 100) %$%
  data.frame(x = x, y = y) %>%
  mutate(area = x >= cutoff)
names(df_dens) <- c("Effect_size", "Frequency", "Published")
p_dark <- ggplot(data = df_dens, aes(x = Effect_size, ymin = 0, ymax = Frequency, fill = Published)) +
  geom_ribbon() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("dark grey", "yellow")) +
  geom_line(aes(y = Frequency)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = cutoff, colour = "red") +
  annotate(geom = 'text', x = cutoff, y = 0.0125, colour = "red", label = 'Significant at p=5%', hjust = -0.1)
print(p_dark)

# remove the significance level criterion
cutoff <- quantile(y, probs = 0.001)

df_dens <- density(y, from = -100, to = 100) %$%
  data.frame(x = x, y = y) %>%
  mutate(area = x >= cutoff)
names(df_dens) <- c("Effect_size", "Frequency", "Published")
p_light <- ggplot(data = df_dens, aes(x = Effect_size, ymin = 0, ymax = Frequency, fill = Published)) +
  geom_ribbon() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("dark grey", "yellow")) +
  geom_line(aes(y = Frequency))
```

Can we only see 5% of the universe?

::: {.notes}
Analogy with dark matter

Meta-analysis - most of it is trying to estimate the unknown latent variable of what is not published
:::

## Misinterpretation of statistics
::: columns
::: {.column width="65%"}
![\label{fig:Ioannidis2005} Ioannidis, 2005, PLOS Medicine](images/Ioannidis2005.png)
:::
::: {.column width="35%"}
- Misinterpretation<br/>of *p* values<br/> as a guide to truth of results
- => High "false discovery rates"
:::
:::


## High "false discovery rates"
Probability of obtaining false positives is greater when:

1. Sample size is small (low "statistical power")
2. Effect size is small low signal:noise
3. Greater number of alternative hypotheses/possible covariates
4. Greater flexibility in designs, definitions, outcomes, and analytical modes
5. Greater vested interests / prejudices
6. Bias - systematic uncertainties in observation process

## Hypothesising after results are known

::: columns
::: {.column width="35%"}
- Exploratory study presented as confirmation
:::

::: {.column width="65%"}
![](images/harking.png){width="80%"}
:::
:::

## Hypothesising after results are known

::: columns
::: {.column width="35%"}
- Hidden multiple testing problem
:::

::: {.column width="65%"}
![](images/significant2.png){width="80%"}
:::
:::


## Hypothesising after results are known
- "Researcher degrees of freedom"
    - many possible choices in data collection & analysis
    - choices favour finding *interesting* patterns
- Motivated cognition
    - "the influence of motives on memory, information processing & reasoning."

::: {.notes}
Selection needn't be deliberate

Andrew Gelman's phrase - forking paths

In psychology, the term "motivated cognition" - we are pre-disposed to find evidence for things we want to believe

Journals want to publish interesting stories
:::

Take 1000 people, only 10 will have it

# Does this apply in ecology?
## Low signal to noise ratio in ecology

- large background variability cf. effect size
- difficulty of measurement
- small sample size
- measurement error
- measurements are a proxy for true process of interest
    - error not propagated

## Publication bias in ecology?
![](images/replication_graph.jpg)

## Same data, many analysts

::: columns
::: {.column width="75%"}
- Experiment in Wytham Woods where brood size is either reduced, increased, or stays the same
- Weight and tarsus length measured for chicks at 14 days old
- Researchers asked: *"To what extent is the growth of nestling blue tits (Cyanistes caeruleus) influenced by competition with siblings?"* 
- Gould et al (2025)
:::
::: {.column width="25%"}
![](images/blue_tit_Oulu.JPG)
![](images/Blue_Tit_Nest.jpg)
:::
:::

## Some decisions to be made....

::: columns 
::: {.column width="60%"}
- What do we use to represent growth?
- What do we use to represent competition with siblings?
- What other variables do we need to take into account?
- How do we take account of the structure of the data (i.e. nests within areas within regions of the wood)?
:::

::: {.column width="40%"}
![](images/forking_paths.png)
:::
:::

## Results

::: columns
::: {.column width="65%"}

- Choice of representation of sibling competition resulted in different ranges of analyst-estimated effects:
- Reduced v unchanged: *-0.05* – *0*
- Enlarged v unchanged: *-0.4* – *-0.15*
- Enlarged v reduced: *-0.7* – *-0.15*
- Count post-change: *-0.55* – *-0.2*
- Change in count: *-0.7* – *-0.3*

:::

::: {.column width="35%"}
![](images/gould_bluetit.png)
:::
:::

## Changing incentives

- Goodhart's Law: *"When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure"*
- San Francisco Declaration on Research Assessment
- Incentivising open sharing of data and code
- Trying to deprioritise "significance" and "novelty"

::: columns
::: {.column width="40%"}
![](images/Wasserstein.png)
:::
::: {.column width="20%"}
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
![](images/Wasserstein2.png)
:::
:::

## Registered reports
![](images/Registered-reports.png){width="50%"}

- publish study design at proposal stage
- allow peer review *before* data collection
- state analysis methods *a priori*
- limits "hypothesising after results are known"
- publish results irrespective of outcome

## Effect of pre-registration

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
Pre-registration dramatically reduces the number of papers where the initial hypothesis is supported by the evidence 
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](images/effect_of_preregistration2.png)
:::
:::

## Many-analyst and multiverse analysis

::: columns 
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Gould et al did a multi-analyst study to evaluate impacts of analyst-choice
- Also possible to do a multiverse analysis where you identify and do all the (reasonable) options yourself (e.g. Risbey et al, 2018)
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
![](images/risbey_multiverse.jpg)
:::
:::
